subject: biology

items.q: What does xylem tissue transport, and in which direction?
items.correct: Water and mineral ions, from the roots to leaves
items.misconception: Dissolved sugars, from the leaves to all parts
items.why: The two tissues are learned together and drawn side by side in the same diagram, so students remember that a plant moves water and food without separating which tissue does which job. Xylem tissue transports water and mineral ions from the roots to the stems and leaves. Phloem tissue transports dissolved sugars from the leaves to the rest of the plant for immediate use or storage.
items.random_wrong: Cell sap, from each living cell to the next one

items.q: How does a root hair cell take up water and mineral ions from the soil?
items.correct: Water enters by osmosis and ions by active transport
items.misconception: Water and mineral ions both enter the cell by osmosis
items.why: Water and mineral ions are absorbed at the same place and at the same time, and osmosis is the transport process students meet first, so it gets used for everything entering the root. Root hair cells are adapted for the efficient uptake of water by osmosis, and mineral ions by active transport. Osmosis moves water only.
items.random_wrong: Water enters by osmosis and sugars by translocation

items.correct: Dissolved sugars move to the rest of the plant
items.misconception: Water and mineral ions move up to the leaves
items.why: The two tissues are learned together and drawn side by side in the same diagram, so students remember that a plant moves water and food without separating which tissue does which job. Xylem tissue transports water and mineral ions from the roots to the stems and leaves. Phloem tissue transports dissolved sugars from the leaves to the rest of the plant for immediate use or storage.
items.random_wrong: Cell sap moves through tubes stiffened by lignin

items.q: What is the role of the guard cells that surround each stoma?
items.correct: They control gas exchange and water loss from the leaf
items.misconception: They are the pores through which gases pass in or out
items.why: The name guard cell sounds like something standing around an opening rather than the opening itself, so the two labels get swapped when a diagram is read. Stomata are pores, with guard cells surrounding stomata. The role of stomata and guard cells is to control gas exchange and water loss.
items.random_wrong: They open more widely when the surrounding air is humid

items.q: A potted plant is moved from a cool, shaded room with still, humid air into a warm, brightly lit room with moving, dry air. What happens to its rate of transpiration?
items.correct: It increases, as water evaporates and diffuses faster
items.misconception: It decreases, as the drier air holds less water vapour
items.why: Students link the idea of more water in the air with more water moving, instead of comparing the water vapour inside the leaf with the water vapour in the air outside. Increasing humidity decreases the rate of transpiration, because water vapour diffuses out of the stomata more slowly when the air outside the leaf already holds a lot of water vapour.
items.random_wrong: It decreases, as the moving air cools the leaf surface

items.q: A student measured the water lost by three identical shoots. Shoot A lost 1.2 cm3 in 60 minutes in still air at 20 degrees C. Shoot B lost 2.4 cm3 in 60 minutes in moving air at 20 degrees C. Shoot C lost 2.0 cm3 in 40 minutes in still air at 30 degrees C. Which conclusion do the results support?
items.correct: The highest rate of water loss was in still air at 30 C
items.misconception: The highest rate of water loss was in moving air at 20 C
items.why: Students compare the numbers in the volume column directly, because the volume is the quantity that was measured and the time taken is recorded separately. The rate of transpiration is a compound measure: it is the volume of water lost divided by the time taken, for example in cm3 per minute, so the times must be taken into account before the shoots are compared.
items.random_wrong: The lowest rate of water loss was in moving air at 20 C

items.q: How is the structure of palisade mesophyll related to its function in a leaf?
items.correct: Its cells contain many chloroplasts that absorb light
items.misconception: Its cells are spread apart to let gases move around
items.why: The two mesophyll names are easily swapped, and the spongy layer often looks larger in a leaf diagram, so students assume it must be doing the main job. Palisade mesophyll cells contain many chloroplasts and are the main photosynthetic tissue of the leaf. Spongy mesophyll cells are loosely packed with air spaces that let gases diffuse.
items.random_wrong: Its cells are hollow tubes made stronger by lignin

items.q: Which statement describes the process of transpiration?
items.correct: Water evaporates from cells and diffuses out of stomata
items.misconception: Sugars dissolve in cells and move down through the xylem
items.why: The two tissues are learned together and drawn side by side in the same diagram, so students remember that a plant moves water and food without separating which tissue does which job. Xylem tissue transports water and mineral ions from the roots to the stems and leaves. Phloem tissue transports dissolved sugars from the leaves to the rest of the plant for immediate use or storage.
items.random_wrong: Water passes out through the guard cells acting as pores

items.q: What happens to the rate of transpiration when air movement across a leaf increases?
items.misconception: Moving air cools a leaf down, so less water evaporates from it and transpiration slows.
items.why: Everyday experience of wind feeling cold is carried over to the leaf, and cooling is correctly linked with slower evaporation, so the wrong overall answer follows from a sensible-looking chain. Increasing air movement increases the rate of transpiration, because moving air carries water vapour away from around the stomata.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What is xylem tissue composed of?
items.misconception: Xylem is made of living cells joined end to end, with pores in the end walls that let cell sap pass from one cell to the next.
items.why: Xylem and phloem are taught in the same breath, so the feature that belongs to phloem, pores in the end walls of elongated cells, is attached to xylem instead. Xylem is composed of hollow tubes strengthened by lignin, adapted for the transport of water in the transpiration stream. It is phloem that is composed of tubes of elongated cells with pores in the end walls.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is a leaf a tissue or an organ?
items.correct: A leaf is a plant organ.
items.misconception: A leaf is a tissue, because it is one thin flat part of the plant made of cells doing the same job.
items.why: The word organ is associated with animals such as the heart or lungs, and a leaf looks like a single uniform sheet from the outside rather than a set of different tissues. The leaf is a plant organ. It is built from several tissues working together: epidermis, palisade and spongy mesophyll, xylem and phloem, and guard cells surrounding stomata.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

specSource: AQA GCSE Biology (8461) specification; section 4.2.3 Plant Tissues, Organs & Systems
